newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: PM WANTS LABOR TO EXPLAIN 1993 COLSTON DEAL
Prime Minister John Howard says the Labor Party needs to explain a 1993 deal put together by Kim Beazley and former Prime Minister Paul Keating to try to get Mal Colston out of the Senate.
Mr Howard's told a function in Brisbane they wanted to send Senator Colston to Norfolk Island and replace him in the Senate with Brian Courtice, who lost his seat at the 1993 poll.
However, he says the deal fell apart when Queensland AWU boss Bill Ludwig intervened, and that seemed to be the real reason why Senator Colston never went to Norfolk Island.
Mr Howard says the deal had more to do with a union giving the thumbs down than high-minded decisions about not sending somebody suspected of rorting travel allowances to Norfolk Island.
PM REITERATES FARMERS NEED CERTAINTY ON LEASES

The Prime Minister says people addressing the Native Title issue have to understand that a breathtaking proportion of Australia is potentially claimable by indigenous people following the Wik decision on native title.
Mr Howard told ABC Radio something like 78 per cent of Australia is potentially claimable post-Wik, and the issue can't just be used for rhetorical responses.
Aboriginal leaders today rejected the government's latest proposal to upgrade pastoral leases, following the High Court's judgement.
Mr Howard says he'll meet Aboriginal leaders on Friday for further negotiations on how to deal with the Wik decision.
PEARSON MUST HONOUR PROMISE ON PASTORAL LEASES-NATIONALS
The Queensland National Party says Noel Pearson, a member of the native title negotiating team, must honour a promise he made four years ago.
The Aboriginal negotiating team supports guaranteeing pastoralists' existing rights, but rejects any wholesale upgrading of pastoral leases.
But National Party President David Russell says Mr Pearson told the National Press Club in 1993 indigenous people would not pursue any rights over pastoral leases in Queensland.
Mr Russell says Mr Pearson told the Press Club Aborigines were satisfied with the facilities available to them under the land fund.
Mr Russell says pastoralists must have exclusive right to their land, which means extinguishing native title.
TELSTRA DEFENDS DIRECTORY ASSISTANCE FEES
Telstra is defending its plan to charge a 75 cent fee on certain directory assistance calls.

Telstra will shortly launch a new service where phone users will have the option of being connected directly to the number they're seeking, rather than having to write the number down and then call it.
Calls to the advanced directory service will initially cost 50 cents but will rise to 75 cents within six months.
A Telstra spokesman says the service will particularly benefit people calling from mobile phones, and as it's optional, does not require Government approval.
Telstra is meanwhile continuing with its push to have a 50 cent fee imposed on all 013 calls, despite the Prime Minister ruling out the initial proposal earlier this year.
ACTU PLANS TO ISOLATE WA
The ACTU has released details of its plan to isolate Western Australia on April the 29th through a communications and transport blockade.
The action is being taken in opposition to new industrial relations legislation in Western Australia, which is before the state's parliament today.
Unionists in Perth yesterday forced the closure of the WA parliament in protests against the laws, aimed at freeing up the industrial system.
An ACTU campaign committee will co-ordinate boycott action in consultation with Western Australian unions and Labor Councils in each state.
ACTU Assistant Secretary Tim Pallas says the new reforms aim to diminish the rights of workers represented in the industrial commission.
Mr Pallas says the ACTU sees the protest against the legislation as a battle for balance in the community.
BRONCOS OWNERS SAYS TOUGH TRADING CONDITIONS WILL CONTINUE
The owners of the Brisbane Broncos league team and the Brisbane Bullets basketball team expect tough trading conditions to continue with sponsorship and gate revenue remaining very tight.
Pacific Sports Entertainment has already reported a loss of six-point-four million dollars for the year but the company's annual report says 1997 should seen an improvement in operating performance.
The company says the high costs of launching the International Triathlon Union world cup series and Superleage will continue to prove a significant drain on profits.
